q: What is an Ethereum Improvement Proposal?
answer: An EIP is a design document that provides information to the Ethereum community or describes a new feature for Ethereum, its processes, or its environment. It must provide a concise technical specification and a rationale for the feature, and its author is responsible for building community consensus and documenting dissenting opinions.
facts: design document
technical specification and rationale
author builds consensus

q: What are the three types of EIP?
answer: There are three types: Standards Track (a change affecting most or all Ethereum implementations), Meta (a process surrounding Ethereum or a change to a process), and Informational (a design issue or general guidelines that users and implementers are free to ignore).
facts: Standards Track
Meta
Informational

q: What are the four categories of a Standards Track EIP?
answer: Standards Track EIPs break down into Core (improvements requiring a consensus fork), Networking (devp2p and light client protocol improvements), Interface (language-level standards such as method names and contract ABIs), and ERC (application-level standards and conventions such as token standards).
facts: Core
Networking
Interface
ERC

q: What statuses can an EIP move through from idea to finished standard?
answer: The standardization process runs Idea (pre-draft, untracked), Draft (first formally tracked stage), Review (author requests peer review), Last Call (final review window), and Final. There are also Stagnant, Withdrawn, and Living statuses outside the main line.
facts: Idea
Draft
Review
Last Call
Final

q: How long is the Last Call review window for an EIP?
answer: An EIP enters Last Call when the specification is stable and the author opens a PR with a review end date — the last-call-deadline — which is typically 14 days later. If that period produces necessary normative changes, the EIP reverts to Review.
facts: last-call-deadline
typically 14 days
reverts to Review on normative changes

q: What happens to an EIP that nobody works on for six months?
answer: Any EIP in Draft, Review, or Last Call that is inactive for six months or more is moved to Stagnant. Authors or EIP editors may resurrect it by moving it back to Draft or its earlier status; if it is not resurrected it may stay in that status forever.
facts: inactive six months or greater
moved to Stagnant
may be resurrected to Draft

q: What does the Living status mean for an EIP, and which EIP is the notable example?
answer: Living is a special status for EIPs designed to be continually updated and never reach a state of finality. EIP-1 itself is the most notable example.
facts: continually updated
never reaches finality
EIP-1 is the example

q: If an author gives up on their proposal permanently, what status applies and can the number be reused?
answer: Withdrawn applies when the authors withdraw the proposed EIP. That state has finality and the EIP can no longer be resurrected using the same EIP number — pursuing the idea later counts as a new proposal.
facts: Withdrawn
has finality
number cannot be reused

q: I have an idea for changing Ethereum. Where do I propose it and how does it become an accepted standard?
answer: Vet the idea with the community first by opening a discussion thread on the Ethereum Magicians forum, then write a formal EIP in the required format. Your role as champion is to shepherd discussions and build community consensus; the EIP is merged as Draft by an editor, then moves through Review and Last Call to Final.
facts: vet idea first
Ethereum Magicians discussion thread
champion builds consensus
Draft to Review to Last Call to Final

q: Who decides how Ethereum standards are proposed, discussed, reviewed, and accepted?
answer: The parties involved are the EIP author (champion), the EIP editors, and the Ethereum Core Developers. Editors handle only the administrative and editorial part and do not pass judgment on EIPs; for Core EIPs, rough consensus among client implementers is reached on AllCoreDevs calls.
facts: author, EIP editors, Core Developers
editors do not pass judgment
AllCoreDevs rough consensus

q: What sections must every successful EIP contain?
answer: An EIP needs a Preamble, Abstract, Specification, Rationale, Security Considerations, and a Copyright Waiver. Motivation, Backwards Compatibility, Test Cases, and Reference Implementation are optional depending on the proposal.
facts: Preamble
Abstract
Specification
Rationale
Security Considerations
Copyright Waiver

q: Is the Security Considerations section optional in an EIP?
answer: No. All EIPs must contain a Security Considerations section — submissions missing it are rejected, and an EIP cannot reach Final status without a Security Considerations discussion the reviewers deem sufficient.
facts: mandatory
submissions missing it are rejected
cannot reach Final without it

q: What is the character limit on an EIP title and description?
answer: The title is limited to a maximum of 44 characters and the description to a maximum of 140 characters. Neither should include the EIP number.
facts: title max 44 characters
description max 140 characters
neither includes the EIP number

q: What goes in the requires header of an EIP?
answer: The requires header lists the EIP numbers that this EIP depends on. A dependency exists when the current EIP cannot be understood or implemented without a concept or technical element from the other EIP; merely mentioning another EIP does not create one.
facts: EIP numbers depended on
cannot be understood or implemented without it
mentioning alone is not a dependency

q: When should I write EIP-X versus ERC-X when referring to a proposal?
answer: When referring to an EIP whose category is ERC, use the hyphenated form ERC-X. For EIPs of any other category, use EIP-X.
facts: ERC category uses ERC-X
other categories use EIP-X

q: Does the discussions-to header accept a link to a GitHub pull request?
answer: No. The preferred discussion URL is a topic on Ethereum Magicians, and the URL cannot point to GitHub pull requests, any ephemeral URL, or any URL that can get locked over time such as Reddit topics.
facts: Ethereum Magicians preferred
cannot be a GitHub pull request
no ephemeral or lockable URLs

q: Do I need to be a named author with an email to submit an EIP, or can I stay anonymous?
answer: Those who prefer anonymity may use a username only, or a first name and a username. At least one author must use a GitHub username so they can be notified on change requests and approve or reject them.
facts: username-only is allowed
at least one author needs a GitHub username
for notification and approval

q: What extra requirement applies to a Core EIP that changes the EVM?
answer: If a Core EIP mentions or proposes changes to the EVM, it should refer to instructions by their mnemonics and define the opcodes of those mnemonics at least once, in the preferred form such as REVERT (0xfe).
facts: refer to instructions by mnemonic
define the opcode at least once

q: Why does a Core EIP need a client implementation before it can be Final?
answer: Core EIPs require client implementations to be considered Final, so the author must either provide an implementation for clients or convince clients to implement the EIP. Presenting on an AllCoreDevs call is the best way to get client implementers to review it.
facts: Core EIPs need client implementations for Final
author provides or convinces clients
AllCoreDevs call for review

q: Can I take over an EIP whose author has gone silent?
answer: Yes. Send a message asking to take over addressed to both the original author and the EIP editor. If the original author does not respond in a timely manner, the EIP editor will make a unilateral decision. Disagreeing with an EIP's direction is a bad reason to transfer ownership — submit a competing EIP instead.
facts: message both original author and editor
editor decides unilaterally if no response
disagreement is not a valid reason

q: Where should images and diagrams for an EIP be stored?
answer: In a subdirectory of the assets folder for that EIP, as assets/eip-N. Link to them with relative links such as ../assets/eip-1/image.png, and prefer SVG diagrams, then PNG, then everything else.
facts: assets/eip-N subdirectory
relative links
prefer SVG then PNG

q: Should RFC 2119 keywords like MUST and SHOULD appear throughout an EIP?
answer: No — the all-caps RFC 2119 keywords should not be used outside the specification section. EIPs are encouraged to follow RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 and to insert the standard interpretation notice at the beginning of the Specification section.
facts: do not use outside the specification section
RFC 2119 and RFC 8174
insert the notice in Specification

q: Why does the EIP process document warn about contentious non-technical issues?
answer: The EIPs process and AllCoreDevs call were not designed to address contentious non-technical issues, but often end up entangled in them for lack of alternatives. That puts the burden on client implementers to gauge community sentiment, which hinders the technical coordination function of EIPs and AllCoreDevs calls.
facts: process not designed for non-technical disputes
burden falls on client implementers
hinders technical coordination

q: What document was the EIP process derived from?
answer: EIP-1 was derived heavily from Bitcoin's BIP-0001 written by Amir Taaki, which in turn was derived from Python's PEP-0001. In many places the text was simply copied and modified.
facts: Bitcoin BIP-0001
which came from Python PEP-0001

q: What is the minimum set of functions an ERC-20 token must implement?
answer: The required methods are totalSupply, balanceOf, transfer, transferFrom, approve, and allowance. name, symbol, and decimals are OPTIONAL — interfaces and other contracts MUST NOT expect those values to be present.
facts: totalSupply, balanceOf, transfer, transferFrom, approve, allowance required
name, symbol, decimals are optional

q: I'm building a game where players can buy coins and spend them on items. How should I represent the coins?
answer: Use ERC-20, the standard interface for tokens. It provides basic functionality to transfer tokens and to approve tokens so they can be spent by another on-chain third party, and its standard interface means any wallet or decentralized exchange can re-use the token.
facts: ERC-20 token standard
transfer and approve for third-party spending
re-usable by wallets and exchanges

q: What do the two events in ERC-20 signal?
answer: Transfer MUST trigger when tokens are transferred, including zero-value transfers, and a contract creating new tokens SHOULD trigger a Transfer with the _from address set to 0x0. Approval MUST trigger on any successful call to approve.
facts: Transfer on any transfer including zero value
minting uses _from = 0x0
Approval on successful approve

q: What does the decimals function on a token actually mean?
answer: decimals returns the number of decimals the token uses — a value of 8, for example, means to divide the token amount by 100000000 to get its user representation. It is an OPTIONAL usability method.
facts: number of decimals used
divide the raw amount to get user representation
optional method

q: Should a token transfer of zero tokens be rejected?
answer: No. Transfers of 0 values MUST be treated as normal transfers and MUST fire the Transfer event. This applies to both transfer and transferFrom.
facts: zero-value transfers are normal transfers
must still fire Transfer

q: What is the difference between transfer and transferFrom in ERC-20?
answer: transfer moves tokens from the message caller's own balance to an address. transferFrom moves tokens from a third address, supporting a withdraw workflow where a contract transfers tokens on your behalf; it SHOULD throw unless the _from account has deliberately authorized the message sender via some mechanism.
facts: transfer sends from the caller
transferFrom is for withdraw workflows
requires prior authorization from _from

q: I want a contract to be able to pull tokens from a user's balance when the user triggers an action. How is that set up?
answer: The user calls approve to allow a spender to withdraw from their account multiple times, up to a value amount, and the spender then calls transferFrom. allowance returns the amount the spender is still allowed to withdraw.
facts: approve sets a spender allowance
spender uses transferFrom
allowance reports the remaining amount

q: What is the known hazard with changing an existing ERC-20 allowance?
answer: Calling approve again overwrites the current allowance with the new value, which opens a documented attack vector. Clients SHOULD build user interfaces that set the allowance to 0 first before setting another value for the same spender, though the contract itself should not enforce this so that pre-existing contracts stay compatible.
facts: approve overwrites the current allowance
set allowance to 0 first in the UI
contract should not enforce it, for backwards compatibility

q: Can I assume an ERC-20 transfer never returns false?
answer: No. Callers MUST handle false from a function returning bool success, and MUST NOT assume that false is never returned.
facts: callers must handle false
must not assume false is never returned

q: Why did anyone bother standardizing a token interface at all?
answer: A standard interface allows any token on Ethereum to be re-used by other applications, from wallets to decentralized exchanges, without each application needing to know the details of each token contract.
facts: standard interface enables re-use
across wallets and decentralized exchanges

q: What does the allowance function tell me?
answer: allowance(_owner, _spender) returns the amount which the spender is still allowed to withdraw from the owner's account.
facts: remaining amount a spender may withdraw

q: Are ERC-20 name and symbol reliable fields to build my UI on?
answer: Not entirely. name and symbol are OPTIONAL methods that can be used to improve usability, but interfaces and other contracts MUST NOT expect these values to be present, so a compliant token may omit them.
facts: name and symbol are optional
must not be assumed present

q: Why do some Ethereum addresses contain both uppercase and lowercase letters?
answer: The mixed case is a checksum. In EIP-55, an address is converted to hex and each letter digit (a-f) is printed uppercase if the corresponding nibble of the keccak256 hash of the lowercase hex address is 8 or higher, otherwise lowercase. The capitalization pattern therefore encodes check bits.
facts: mixed case encodes a checksum
letters uppercased based on the hash nibble
hash of the lowercase hex address

q: I want to make sure a user hasn't accidentally typed an invalid Ethereum address before sending money.
answer: Validate the EIP-55 mixed-case checksum: re-derive the expected capitalization from the keccak256 hash of the lowercase hex address and compare it to what was entered. A mistyped randomly generated address has only about a 0.0247% net probability of accidentally passing the check.
facts: re-derive the checksum capitalization
compare against the entered address
about 0.0247% chance a mistype passes

q: Exactly how does EIP-55 decide which letters to capitalize?
answer: Hash the lowercase hexadecimal address with keccak256, treating the hex address as ASCII/UTF-8 text. For each character position i, if the character is a decimal digit leave it alone; if it is a letter a-f, print it uppercase when the hash nibble at that same position is greater than 7, otherwise lowercase.
facts: keccak256 of the lowercase hex address as ASCII
digits 0-9 are unchanged
letter uppercased when the hash nibble is 8 or higher

q: What exactly gets fed into the keccak256 hash when computing an address checksum?
answer: The input is the lowercase hexadecimal string itself — the hex address encoded as ASCII — not the 20 raw bytes of the address. The reference implementation notes this explicitly.
facts: input is the lowercase hex string
encoded as ASCII, not raw bytes

q: How strong is the EIP-55 checksum, and how does it compare to alternatives?
answer: There are on average 15 check bits per address, and the net probability that a randomly generated mistyped address accidentally passes is 0.0247%. That is roughly a 50x improvement over ICAP, but not as good as a 4-byte check code.
facts: about 15 check bits on average
0.0247% false-pass probability
~50x better than ICAP, weaker than a 4-byte check code

q: Why was a mixed-case checksum chosen instead of adding extra characters to the address?
answer: It is backwards compatible with many hex parsers that already accept mixed case, allowing gradual introduction, and it keeps the address length at 40 characters rather than growing it.
facts: backwards compatible with mixed-case hex parsers
can be introduced over time
keeps length at 40 characters

q: Is an all-lowercase Ethereum address valid?
answer: Yes — the test cases include all-lowercase and all-caps addresses as valid, because for some addresses the derived checksum happens to produce no mixed case. An address whose case pattern does not match the derived checksum is what indicates a likely error.
facts: all-lower and all-caps cases exist in the test vectors
mismatch with the derived pattern indicates an error

q: A user pasted an Ethereum address into my application. How can I detect likely typing mistakes?
answer: Run the address through the EIP-55 checksum encoder: lowercase it, hash it with keccak256, and rebuild the capitalization. If the rebuilt string does not equal what the user pasted, the address is very likely mistyped.
facts: recompute the checksum encoding
compare to the pasted string
mismatch means likely mistype

q: What happens if an address contains a character that isn't valid hex?
answer: The reference implementation raises a validation error, reporting the unrecognized hex character and its position, rather than producing a checksummed output.
facts: raises a validation error
reports the character and position

q: What is the purpose of the supportsInterface function?
answer: supportsInterface(bytes4 interfaceID) lets a contract publish which interfaces it implements so callers can detect them. It returns true when the interfaceID is one the contract implements, true for 0x01ffc9a7 (ERC-165 itself), and false for 0xffffffff and any other interfaceID.
facts: publishes implemented interfaces
true for 0x01ffc9a7
false for 0xffffffff

q: My application needs to know whether another contract supports a particular feature before calling it. How can it check?
answer: Use ERC-165. First confirm the target implements ERC-165, then simply call supportsInterface(interfaceID) with the identifier of the interface you want. If the contract does not implement ERC-165, you have to determine its methods the old-fashioned way.
facts: confirm ERC-165 support first
then call supportsInterface with the interface id
otherwise no standard way to detect

q: What is the ERC-165 interface identifier, and how is it derived?
answer: It is 0x01ffc9a7, calculated as bytes4(keccak256('supportsInterface(bytes4)')).
facts: 0x01ffc9a7
bytes4 of keccak256 of the function signature

q: How is an interface identifier computed in ERC-165?
answer: An interface is a set of function selectors as defined by the Ethereum ABI, and the interface identifier is the XOR of all function selectors in the interface. Optional functions are not permitted in an interface, so they never contribute to the identity.
facts: XOR of all function selectors
selectors as defined by the Ethereum ABI
optional functions are excluded

q: What is the exact procedure for detecting whether a contract implements ERC-165 at all?
answer: Make a STATICCALL with 30,000 gas to supportsInterface(0x01ffc9a7). If it fails or returns false, the contract does not implement ERC-165. If it returns true, make a second call with supportsInterface(0xffffffff); if that fails or returns true, the contract does not implement ERC-165. Otherwise it does.
facts: STATICCALL with 30,000 gas
first call supportsInterface(0x01ffc9a7)
second call supportsInterface(0xffffffff) must return false

q: Why does the ERC-165 detection procedure bother making a second call with 0xffffffff?
answer: The 0xffffffff probe catches contracts that return true for everything. A genuine ERC-165 implementation must return false for 0xffffffff, so a true answer there proves the contract is not really implementing the standard. This mechanism also works with most pre-standard contracts to show they do not implement ERC-165.
facts: 0xffffffff must return false
detects contracts that answer true to everything
also works against pre-standard contracts

q: Is there a gas limit on supportsInterface?
answer: Yes — the function must return a bool and use at most 30,000 gas, and the detection procedure calls it with exactly 30,000 gas.
facts: at most 30,000 gas
detection calls it with 30,000 gas

q: Should I implement supportsInterface with a mapping or with a chain of comparisons?
answer: The view mapping implementation costs 586 gas for any input but requires an SSTORE (20,000 gas) per interface at initialization. The pure comparison implementation costs 236 gas at worst but grows linearly with the number of interfaces. With three or more supported interfaces — counting ERC-165 itself — the mapping approach costs less gas in every case than the pure approach at its worst case.
facts: mapping: 586 gas per call, 20,000 gas SSTORE per interface at init
pure: 236 gas worst case, grows linearly
mapping wins at three or more interfaces

q: I have a contract address, but I don't know what kind of functionality it supports. Is there a standard way to find out?
answer: Yes — ERC-165 standardizes interface detection. If the contract implements ERC-165 you can call supportsInterface with the identifier of any interface you care about to learn whether it is supported.
facts: ERC-165 standard interface detection
call supportsInterface with an interface id

q: Why was interface detection needed in the first place?
answer: For standard interfaces such as ERC-20 it is useful to query whether a contract supports the interface, and which version, in order to adapt how the contract is interacted with. ERC-165 standardizes the concept of an interface and the identification of interfaces.
facts: query support to adapt interaction
standardizes interface identification

q: One mapping entry in an ERC-165 implementation must never be set to true. Which one and why?
answer: Element 0xffffffff must not be set to true. The detection procedure relies on supportsInterface(0xffffffff) returning false to prove a contract genuinely implements ERC-165, so setting it would break detection.
facts: 0xffffffff must not be true
detection depends on it returning false

q: I want my application to behave differently depending on what capabilities another contract provides.
answer: ERC-165 is the mechanism for that: query the contract with supportsInterface for each interface identifier your application can take advantage of, and branch on the answers. That is exactly the use case the standard cites — adapting the way a contract is interacted with.
facts: query supportsInterface per interface id
branch on the results
adapting interaction is the cited motivation

q: I want users to sign an agreement, but I want the wallet to clearly show what they are agreeing to instead of displaying unreadable data.
answer: EIP-712 is the standard for hashing and signing typed structured data rather than opaque bytestrings. It encodes data along with its structure so the wallet can display the fields to the user for verification when signing, instead of showing an opaque hex string with little context.
facts: typed structured data instead of bytestrings
structure allows display for verification
replaces the opaque hex string

q: How can I create a human-readable signing request for something like 'buy this item for 5 tokens'?
answer: Define a Solidity-like struct for the message, then have the wallet sign it with eth_signTypedData following EIP-712. The struct's type and field names travel with the data, so the user-agent can present each field rather than a hash.
facts: define a struct type
sign with eth_signTypedData
fields are presentable to the user

q: My users keep getting confused by long strings of random-looking data when signing things. How can I make signing safer and easier to understand?
answer: Adopt EIP-712. The motivation for the standard is exactly this: signed messages are currently an opaque hex string shown with little context about the items making up the message, and hashing structured data by hand is non-trivial with errors costing the system's security properties.
facts: opaque hex string is the stated problem
structured data can be displayed
hand-rolled hashing loses security properties

q: How is a typed structured message encoded before signing under EIP-712?
answer: encode(domainSeparator, message) = "\x19\x01" || domainSeparator || hashStruct(message). The 0x19 prefix and 0x01 version byte make it ERC-191 compliant, with the domain separator as the version-specific data and the 32-byte hashStruct as the data to sign.
facts: \x19\x01 prefix
domainSeparator concatenated with hashStruct(message)
ERC-191 compliant with version byte 0x01

q: Why does EIP-712 use a domain separator?
answer: It prevents collisions between otherwise identical structures: two DApps could define the same struct such as Transfer(address from,address to,uint256 amount) that should not be signature-compatible. The domain separator also allows multiple distinct signing use cases on the same struct instance within one DApp.
facts: prevents cross-DApp signature collisions
identical structs should not be compatible
allows distinct use cases on the same struct

q: What fields can go into the EIP-712 domain?
answer: The EIP712Domain struct may contain string name, string version, uint256 chainId, address verifyingContract, and bytes32 salt. Protocol designers include only the fields that make sense for their signing domain, and unused fields are left out of the struct type entirely.
facts: name, version, chainId, verifyingContract, salt
only relevant fields are included
unused fields are omitted from the type

q: What should a wallet do if the chainId in a typed data domain does not match the active chain?
answer: The chainId field is the EIP-155 chain id, and the user-agent should refuse signing if it does not match the currently active chain. Similarly, verifyingContract lets the user-agent do contract-specific phishing prevention.
facts: chainId is the EIP-155 chain id
user-agent should refuse to sign on mismatch
verifyingContract enables phishing prevention

q: How is hashStruct defined in EIP-712?
answer: hashStruct(s) = keccak256(typeHash || encodeData(s)), where typeHash = keccak256(encodeType(typeOf(s))). The typeHash is a constant for a given struct type and does not need to be computed at runtime.
facts: keccak256 of typeHash concatenated with encodeData
typeHash is keccak256 of encodeType
typeHash is a compile-time constant

q: How does EIP-712 encode a struct's type into a string?
answer: The type is encoded as name("member₁,member₂,...") with each member written as type followed by a space and its name — for example Mail(address from,address to,string contents). Referenced struct types are collected, sorted by name, and appended, producing encodings like Transaction(Person from,Person to,Asset tx)Asset(address token,uint256 amount)Person(address wallet,string name).
facts: name followed by parenthesized member list
each member is type space name
referenced structs sorted by name and appended

q: How are strings and byte arrays encoded inside EIP-712 struct data?
answer: The dynamic values bytes and string are encoded as the keccak256 hash of their contents, so each encoded member value stays exactly 32 bytes long.
facts: bytes and string are hashed with keccak256
every encoded member is 32 bytes

q: How does EIP-712 encode arrays inside a struct?
answer: Array values are encoded as the keccak256 hash of the concatenated encodeData of their contents — the encoding of SomeType[5] is identical to that of a struct containing five members of type SomeType.
facts: keccak256 of concatenated encodeData of the elements
SomeType[5] encodes like a five-member struct

q: What are the atomic types allowed by EIP-712?
answer: The atomic types are bytes1 through bytes32, uint8 through uint256, int8 through int256, bool, and address. There are no uint or int aliases, contract addresses are always plain address, and fixed point numbers are not supported.
facts: bytes1-bytes32, uint8-uint256, int8-int256, bool, address
no uint or int aliases
fixed point is not supported

q: Can I sign a recursive or cyclical data structure with EIP-712?
answer: Recursive struct types are supported by the type system, but the encoding is optimized for tree-like data and is undefined for cyclical data. Supporting cycles was considered and rejected as prohibitively complex, and it would break the composability of building a struct's hash from its members' hashes.
facts: recursive struct types are supported
encoding is undefined for cyclical data
rejected as too complex and breaking composability

q: Why did EIP-712 not just use ABIv2 function signatures for the type hash?
answer: bytes4 is not collision resistant enough, and unlike function signatures there is negligible runtime cost to a longer hash. A 256-bit ABIv2 signature would capture type info but not semantics — that is already causing a practical collision between ERC-20's and ERC-721's transfer(address,uint256), where the uint256 is an amount in one and a unique id in the other.
facts: bytes4 is not collision resistant
longer hashes cost little at runtime
ERC-20 vs ERC-721 transfer(address,uint256) collision

q: Why is tight packing not used for EIP-712's encodeData?
answer: Tight packing — Solidity's default when calling keccak256 with multiple arguments — minimizes bytes hashed but requires complicated packing instructions in the EVM and does not allow in-place computation. Plain ABIv2 encoding was also rejected because it is non-deterministic: several valid ABIv2 encodings exist for the same data.
facts: tight packing blocks in-place computation
needs complicated EVM packing
ABIv2 fails the determinism criterion

q: Does EIP-712 protect me against a signature being used twice?
answer: No. The standard explicitly does not include replay protection — it covers only signing messages and verifying signatures. Implementers must make sure the application behaves correctly when it sees the same signed message twice, by rejecting the repeat or making the action idempotent.
facts: no replay protection in the standard
implementer must reject repeats or be idempotent

q: What frontrunning risk does EIP-712 warn about?
answer: An attacker can intercept a signature and submit it to the contract before the original intended use takes place. The mechanism for broadcasting a signature is application-specific, so the application must behave correctly when an attacker submits first — by rejecting it or producing exactly the effect the signer intended.
facts: attacker submits the intercepted signature first
broadcast mechanism is out of scope
reject or produce the intended effect

q: Is it safe to write keccak256(someStruct) in Solidity?
answer: No. That expression is valid syntax but evaluates to the keccak256 hash of the memory address of the instance. EIP-712 calls this behaviour dangerous — it can appear to work in some scenarios while failing determinism and injectiveness in others, and DApps depending on it should be considered dangerously broken.
facts: hashes the memory address, not the contents
fails determinism and injectiveness
dependent DApps are dangerously broken

q: Why can't EIP-712 signing start directly with the domain separator or typeHash?
answer: Because the encoding must stay injective across all signable message types. The first byte distinguishes the cases, and while hard, it may be possible to construct a typeHash that also happens to be a prefix of a valid RLP encoded transaction.
facts: first byte distinguishes the cases
a typeHash could prefix a valid RLP transaction
injectiveness would be lost

q: What is the difference between how a plain text message and a typed struct are prepared for signing?
answer: A bytestring is encoded as "\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n" followed by the non-zero-padded ascii-decimal length and then the message. Typed structured data is encoded as "\x19\x01" followed by the domain separator and hashStruct(message). Both begin with 0x19, and a transaction's RLP encoding does not, which keeps the three cases distinguishable.
facts: personal message uses the Ethereum Signed Message prefix with length
typed data uses \x19\x01 with domain separator
RLP transactions do not start with 0x19

q: Can a DApp add its own custom fields to the EIP-712 domain?
answer: No — DApp implementers should not add private fields; new fields should be proposed through the EIP process. Future field additions must be in alphabetical order and come after the existing fields, and user-agents should accept fields in any order as specified by the EIP712Domain type.
facts: no private fields
new fields go through the EIP process
future additions come after, alphabetically

q: I want every sword in my game to be a unique item that belongs to one player and can be sold to another.
answer: Use ERC-721, the non-fungible token standard. It provides a standard API to track and transfer NFTs where each asset is distinguishable and its ownership is tracked separately, and it supports transfers by the owner, an approved address, or an authorized operator.
facts: ERC-721 non-fungible token standard
each asset is distinguishable, ownership tracked separately
owner, approved address, or operator may transfer

throws if _from is not the owner

q: Does ERC-721 scale to very large numbers of tokens?

q: What kinds of assets did ERC-721's authors intend it to represent?

q: Why is ERC-20 insufficient for tracking NFTs?

q: Must a contract implementing ERC721Metadata also implement the core ERC721 interface?

ERC-721 implies ERC-165

q: My game has gold, health potions, bullets, and rare weapons. Some items are identical and others are unique. How should I represent them?

With blockchain games creating thousands of token types, a standard supporting them was needed.

q: What does the _id argument mean in ERC-1155 functions?

each id is its own configurable type

q: Which events must an ERC-1155 contract emit when balances change?

q: What must a contract return to accept an ERC-1155 transfer?

q: What is the ERC-165 identifier for the ERC-1155 token receiver interface?

q: When exactly is the ERC-1155 receiver hook called relative to the balance update?

q: Why does ERC-1155 support single transfers when it already has batch transfers?

facts: single transfers are significantly cheaper

receivers can rely on the hook always firing

q: How does the {id} substitution in an ERC-1155 URI work?

lowercase, no 0x prefix, padded to 64 characters
lets many tokens share one on-chain string

q: What is the ERC-165 identifier for the ERC-1155 metadata URI extension?

q: Why did ERC-1155 drop the name and symbol functions?

q: What does setApprovalForAll do in ERC-1155, and how do I approve only some token ids?

no self-approval required

q: What does balanceOfBatch give me over balanceOf?

If it fails or does not return true, assume the recipient is not an ERC1155TokenReceiver and follow the other standard's transfer rules — but the ERC-1155 transfer events MUST still be emitted so balances remain derivable from events.

fall back to the other standard's rules on failure

callers check validity on the contract's behalf

q: Which kinds of contracts should implement ERC-1271?

DAOs

orders are signed messages
contracts cannot sign without a private key

q: What is the difference between the base fee and priority fee introduced by EIP-1559?
answer: The base fee per gas is a fixed-per-block network fee set by protocol and is always burned. The priority fee is what the transaction offers to the block producer to incentivize inclusion. Senders always pay the base fee of the block their transaction lands in plus the priority fee they set, as long as the combined amount does not exceed the transaction's max fee per gas.

priority fee goes to the block producer
total is capped by max fee per gas

q: Why does sending a transaction sometimes involve a base fee and another amount paid to the block producer?
answer: EIP-1559 replaced the simple first-price auction with a protocol-set base fee that adjusts with congestion and is burned, plus a priority fee the sender offers the block producer. Because base fee changes are constrained and predictable, wallets can auto-set fees reliably and most users need only add a small priority fee.

priority fee incentivizes the producer
constrained changes let wallets auto-set fees

q: How does Ethereum decide how much of a transaction fee is burned and how much goes to the validator?

q: What is the transaction format introduced by EIP-1559?

q: How fast can the base fee change from one block to the next?
answer: BASE_FEE_MAX_CHANGE_DENOMINATOR is 8, so the base fee can move by at most one eighth — 12.5% — per block, computed as parent_base_fee_per_gas * gas_used_delta // parent_gas_target // 8. Because the changes are constrained, the maximum block-to-block difference is predictable.
facts: BASE_FEE_MAX_CHANGE_DENOMINATOR is 8
at most a 1/8 change per block
predictability is the design goal

q: What is the gas target in EIP-1559 and how does it relate to the block gas limit?

ELASTICITY_MULTIPLIER is 2
base fee rises above target and falls below it

q: What is the initial base fee value at the EIP-1559 fork block?

q: What was wrong with Ethereum's original first-price gas auction?
answer: Four problems: transaction fee volatility bore no relation to the social cost of a transaction; the hard per-block gas limit caused needless multi-block delays with no slack mechanism; first price auctions are well known to be inefficient and force complex fee estimation that still leads to frequent overpayment; and blockchains with no issuance that reward miners entirely through fees face instability, including incentives to mine sister blocks and stronger selfish mining attacks.

no slack mechanism, so needless delays
first-price auctions are inefficient

q: Why is the base fee burned rather than paid to the miner?
answer: Burning it ensures only ETH can ever be used to pay for transactions on Ethereum, cementing ETH's economic value and reducing risks associated with miner extractable value. Critically, a miner who does not receive the base fee has no incentive to manipulate the fee in order to extract more from users. The burn also counterbalances inflation while the block reward and priority fee still go to miners.

removes the incentive to manipulate the fee
counterbalances inflation

q: What did EIP-1559 change about the GASPRICE opcode?

previously it meant both paid and received

q: Do legacy transactions still work after EIP-1559?

q: Does EIP-1559 change the block hash computation?

q: How is transaction ordering affected when most users stop competing on fees?

It is recommended that transactions with equal priority fees be sorted by the time received, to protect against spamming attacks where an attacker floods the pending pool so at least one transaction lands favorably.

q: Could miners attack EIP-1559 by mining empty blocks?
answer: It is possible but not a stable equilibrium while mining is decentralized: any defector earns more than a participant for as long as the attack continues, even after the base fee reaches 0. Since defection is anonymous and unprovable, an attacker needs over 50% of hashing power — at which point double spending or ignoring other miners is far more profitable. The elasticity multiplier can also be increased to raise the bar.

defectors profit more, anonymously

q: Does EIP-1559 mean ETH has a fixed supply?
answer: No — by burning the base fee, a fixed Ether supply can no longer be guaranteed. If more is burned than is generated in rewards ETH is deflationary, and if less, inflationary. Since user demand for block space cannot be controlled, neither outcome can be asserted in advance, so core developers lose some control over Ether's long-term quantity.

q: What risk does EIP-1559's larger maximum block size introduce?

Over time the average block size should remain about the same, so this is only an issue for short-term bursts, but a client that handles bursts poorly could error — for example out of memory — so clients should ensure they handle individual blocks up to the maximum size.

q: How are transaction fees handled differently before and after Ethereum's newer fee-market design?
answer: Before, users bid a gasprice in a first-price auction, miners picked the highest bids, and everyone paid what they bid — with all of it going to the miner. After EIP-1559, a protocol-set base fee that adjusts with congestion is burned, the sender adds a priority fee for the producer, and a max fee bounds the total.

after: protocol base fee burned plus priority fee

q: Can someone else pay the network fee for my users while the users still approve the action?

q: What are the four roles defined in ERC-2771?

The Recipient then checks that the forwarder is trusted, extracts the address from the last 20 bytes of the calldata and uses it as the original sender, and if msg.sender is not a trusted forwarder or msg.data is shorter than 20 bytes it returns the original msg.sender as-is.

This matters most at the Web3 wallet level, since wallets may know nothing about the recipient contract. If a forwarder is upgradeable you must also trust it will not perform a malicious upgrade. Changing which forwarders are trusted must be restricted, since an attacker who could trust their own address could forge transactions — the list is recommended to be immutable, or else modifiable only by trusted contract owners.

Standardizing the simplest viable interface makes it easy to add support, gives clients a standard way to discover support and to send meta transactions, and by staying agnostic to the forwarder's internals lets a recipient support multiple forwarders with no code change.

q: I want someone to be able to submit an action for another user, as long as the user has already approved that action.
answer: ERC-2771 covers exactly that: the user is the Transaction Signer who authorizes the request, and an untrusted third party — the Gas Relay — pays the gas and relays it through a Trusted Forwarder, which verifies signatures and nonces before forwarding to the recipient.

q: What is the role of a bundler in ERC-4337?

q: What is a UserOperation and how does it differ from a transaction?

Like a transaction it has to, calldata, maxFeePerGas, maxPriorityFeePerGas, nonce, and signature — but it carries several extra fields, and notably the signature field's usage is defined by the Smart Contract Account implementation rather than by the protocol.

q: Does ERC-4337 require changes to Ethereum consensus?
answer: No — it completely avoids the need for consensus-layer protocol changes. That was a deliberate goal, since consensus development is focused on scalability features and there may not be an opportunity for further protocol changes for a long time, so avoiding them increases the chance of faster adoption.

deliberate design goal

q: I want my application to let users perform several actions without requiring them to manage a traditional wallet account in the usual way.

q: What is the EntryPoint contract in ERC-4337?

handleOps takes the ops array and a beneficiary

q: What is a paymaster in ERC-4337?
answer: A helper contract that agrees to pay for a transaction instead of the sender. Paymasters let application developers subsidize fees for their users, let users pay fees with ERC-20 tokens, and support many other use cases. They follow a pre-charge and later refund model — a token paymaster may pre-charge the maximum possible price and refund the excess afterwards.

pre-charge then refund model

q: How does the two-dimensional nonce in ERC-4337 work?
answer: The single uint256 nonce is treated as two values: a 192-bit key and a 64-bit sequence. For each key the EntryPoint validates the sequence, which increments sequentially and monotonically per sender; a new key can be introduced with an arbitrary value at any time with its sequence starting at 0. getNonce(address sender, uint192 key) exposes these values. This preserves on-chain UserOperation hash uniqueness while letting accounts implement custom ordering logic.

sequence increments monotonically per key

confines it to the sequence with a zero key

q: What is an aggregator in ERC-4337?

full design is out of scope

q: What is a factory in ERC-4337 and how must it create accounts?

It is expected to use CREATE2 (0xF5) rather than CREATE (0xF0) so creation order does not affect generated addresses, and it should return the account address even if it was already created. All factory contracts MUST check that calls to createAccount() originate from the entryPoint.senderCreator() address, and a factory accessing global storage has to be staked.

q: Why must an ERC-4337 account address depend on its initial signature?
answer: For security: if the address did not depend on the initial signature, someone else could deploy an account at that address and set different credentials to control it. Making the generated contract address depend on the initial signature prevents that.

address must depend on the initial signature

That gives the counterfactual address, so a user can generate an address locally and immediately start accepting funds without needing any custom action or an existing user to create the account.

gives the counterfactual address

q: Why isn't initCode called directly from the EntryPoint in ERC-4337?

so initCode runs from another address

q: What are the ERC-4337 error code prefixes and what do they mean?

AA1 signifies an error during sender creation, AA2 during sender validation in validateUserOp, and AA3 during paymaster validation in validatePaymasterUserOp. The EntryPoint must only revert with explicit SignatureValidationFailed(), FailedOp(), or FailedOpWithRevert() errors.

The bundler must also track each paymaster's balance while adding operations to ensure it can pay for all operations using it.

q: What should a bundler do before including an ERC-4337 bundle in a block?

If it reverts, use the trace to find the offending entity — the last entity CALL'ed by the EntryPoint before the revert — remove that UserOperation from the bundle and mempool, ban the guilty factory or paymaster unless the sender is staked (in which case ban the sender), and repeat until the trace succeeds.

q: Why does ERC-4337 need a reputation and staking system?
answer: Storage access rules stop UserOperations from interfering with each other, but global entities — paymasters and factories — are accessed by many operations and could invalidate many previously valid ones. Such entities are throttled or banned, and staking makes a Sybil attack expensive. The stake is never slashed; its only use is Sybil resistance, it can be withdrawn after the unstake delay, and it is enforced by each bundler during simulation rather than on chain.

staking prevents Sybil attacks

q: What is the core DoS problem ERC-4337 has to solve?
answer: How a block builder can be sure an operation will actually pay fees without first executing the whole thing. Requiring full execution opens a DoS vector, since an attacker could send many operations that appear to pay but revert at the last moment after long execution. The answer is a clean separation of validation from execution: accounts expose validateUserOp, which verifies the signature and pays the fee, and only if it succeeds does execution happen.

attackers could revert after long execution

q: What is an alternative mempool in ERC-4337?

And safety against fee draining — if the EntryPoint calls validateUserOp and it passes, it must also make the generic call with calldata equal to userOp.calldata.

safety against fee draining

If such an account has a function for authorizing a trusted UserOperation submitter, the gap can be bridged by creating an ERC-4337 compatible account that re-implements the verification logic as a wrapper and setting it as the original account's trusted submitter.

q: Why does concentrating logic in the ERC-4337 EntryPoint reduce total audit burden?
answer: Because individual accounts have much less to do — they need only verify validateUserOp and its check-signature-and-pay-fees logic, and check that other functions are gated on msg.sender == ENTRY_POINT, perhaps also allowing msg.sender == self. The trade-off is that security risk is concentrated in the EntryPoint, which must be audited and formally verified since it is a central trust point for everything.

risk concentrates in the EntryPoint
EntryPoint needs auditing and formal verification

q: Why must an ERC-4337 signature depend on the chainid and EntryPoint address?
answer: To prevent replay attacks, either cross-chain or across multiple EntryPoint contract versions.

prevents replay across EntryPoint versions

q: What is the PackedUserOperation and why does it exist?

It concatenates fields into fewer slots: initCode joins the factory address and factoryData, accountGasLimits packs verificationGasLimit and callGasLimit into 16 bytes each, gasFees packs maxPriorityFeePerGas and maxFeePerGas into 16 bytes each, and paymasterAndData concatenates the paymaster fields.

q: What is in the paymasterAndData field?

q: What is a deposit in ERC-4337?

q: What is the front-running initialization risk in EIP-7702?
answer: Contracts are normally deployed by executing initcode, which lets developers initialize storage slots in a way an observer cannot replace. EIP-7702 gives no opportunity to run initcode or set storage during delegation, so an observer could front-run initialization with an account they control.
